wine.name: Don Maximiano Founder's Reserve
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, the larger part, with Malbec, Carmenère, Petit Verdot and in some years Cabernet Franc, in shares that change with the vintage.
wine.sites: The historic Don Maximiano estate at Panquehue, in the warm inland Aconcagua valley: the Max I and Max II blocks on hillsides facing north and north east, on weathered diorite, an igneous rock, and Max V on a stony alluvial terrace close to the Aconcagua river, cooler than the slopes.
wine.making: The house's sheets give about twenty two months in French oak barrels for the vintages from 2015, between three fifths and three quarters of them new, with a share in large Stockinger casks in 2020. Earlier wines had less wood: sixteen months for the 1995, twenty months in new oak for the 2008.
wine.glass: Cassis, blackberry and black cherry over cedar, graphite and dried mountain herbs, with a touch of cocoa; full and firm, its fine, ripe tannin carried by a warm valley's weight and a long, savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Closed for its first few years, it opens after about a decade in a strong vintage and keeps for twenty years and more.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or two, an old one gently off its sediment; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The wine is named for Maximiano Errázuriz, who founded the house at Panquehue in 1870.
The denomination of the valley north of Santiago, warm inland at Panquehue and cool at the coast.
The second wine of the same estate, a different label from the Founder's Reserve.

records.table: From the estate the founder planted at Panquehue in 1870 comes Viña Errázuriz's Don Maximiano Founder's Reserve: Cabernet Sauvignon led, with Malbec and Carmenère, aged about two years in French oak. Cedar and cassis on firm tannin, so decant it.
records.story: Panquehue, in the Aconcagua valley, is where Maximiano Errázuriz (1832 to 1890), a surveyor, politician and industrialist of a leading Santiago family, bought land and planted vines in 1870, the year the house dates itself. By its own account he was the first to bring French grape varieties to the valley, at a time when most of Chile's vineyards lay close to Santiago, some hundred kilometres to the south. The estate keeps its historic underground cellars, built of lime and stone masonry more than a century ago. The house stayed with his descendants, and the family behind Viñedo Chadwick in the Maipo and Seña on the Aconcagua slopes is of the same line. Don Maximiano Founder's Reserve, the red named for him, was first released, by two accounts, with the 1984 vintage, a Cabernet Sauvignon alone from the blocks of his estate, and over the years it became a blend led by Cabernet with Malbec, Carmenère and Petit Verdot. In 2020 the house marked its hundred and fiftieth year with a vertical tasting of the wine. It is the founder's wine of the valley, warm, firm and long lived, a world away from the house's cool coastal whites of the Aconcagua Costa.

records.place: Lo Abarca, San Antonio Valley, Chile

wine.name: Cipreses Vineyard Sauvignon Blanc
wine.sites: The Cipreses vineyard on the slopes at Lo Abarca, about four kilometres from the Pacific, on poor soils of limestone and granite, swept by the cold winds of the Humboldt Current.
wine.making: Picked by hand, usually in April, from vines planted around the turn of the century. By the house's sheets the grapes are pressed gently, as whole bunches in some vintages and after a few hours on their skins in others; the juice ferments cool in stainless steel and rests on its fine lees, with no correction of acidity, and in some vintages a small share spends a few months in French oak.
wine.glass: Lime, grapefruit pith and gooseberry over cut grass, green pepper and a salty, sea spray edge; taut and bone dry, with high, keen acidity and a long, chalky finish.
wine.ageing: Bright and sharp on release, it holds and gains texture for five years and more, its low pH and high acidity keeping it fresh.
wine.serve: 10 degrees Celsius, or a little cooler; no need to decant; a white wine glass.

label.means: The single vineyard on the Lo Abarca slopes from which this Sauvignon Blanc is drawn.
The coastal village of the estate, recognised as its own denomination of origin in 2018.
The coastal valley of the Aconcagua region, south of Casablanca and closer to the sea.

records.table: Four kilometres from the Pacific, on limestone and granite slopes at Lo Abarca, grows Casa Marín's Cipreses Vineyard Sauvignon Blanc: lime, grapefruit and cut grass with a salty edge and keen acidity. Pour it cold beside shellfish.
records.story: In 2000 the founder of Casa Marín, a winemaker who by the house's account became the first woman to found and own a winery in Chile, chose to make high end white wines, at a time when Chilean fine wine meant warm valley reds. She planted at Lo Abarca, a village of the San Antonio Valley about four kilometres from the Pacific, on coastal ground that many thought too cold and windy for vines. The slopes are steep, the soils poor limestone and granite, and the Humboldt Current sends cold winds and fog in from the sea, so the vines ripen slowly and keep their acidity. Sauvignon Blanc was the estate's purpose from the start, and Cipreses Vineyard became its flagship, beside a peppery Syrah, a Pinot Noir and a Riesling from the same hills. In 2018 Lo Abarca was recognised as a denomination of origin, and Casa Marín, the only producer there, became the first Chilean winery to hold a denomination of its own. Cipreses teaches the coast: latitude says warm, but the cold ocean gives a Sauvignon Blanc of keen acidity, citrus and salt, picked as late as April.

records.place: Leyda, Leyda Valley, San Antonio, Chile

wine.name: Lot 21 Pinot Noir
wine.grapes: Pinot Noir alone, clone 777 among its vines.
wine.sites: Estate plots in the Leyda hills close to the Pacific, cooled by the sea breeze, on mixed soils of granite, clay and lime; early vintages came from one block of the El Maitén vineyard, later ones from three plots.
wine.making: Each plot is picked and fermented on its own, by the accounts read with native yeasts in closed concrete vats and a share of whole bunches that changes by vintage. The wine is then raised mostly in large untoasted foudres, with concrete and some used 300 litre French oak barrels; the house keeps barrel ageing light across its reds.
wine.glass: Red cherry, raspberry and rose hip over dried thyme, forest floor and a saline, iodine note; light in body and silky, with fine tannin, fresh acidity and a long, savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Open and fragrant within two or three years, it gains forest floor and spice over the following five to eight.
wine.serve: 13 to 15 degrees Celsius; no need to decant, though a young bottle opens with a little air; a Burgundy glass.

label.means: The house's small lot line, at the head of its range, drawn from a selection of its plots.
The coastal denomination of 2002 within the San Antonio Valley, south of Casablanca.

records.table: Concrete vats, some whole bunches and large foudres shape Lot 21, Viña Leyda's Pinot Noir from estate plots in the Leyda hills near the Pacific: cherry, rose hip and a salty, savoury edge. Serve it just below room temperature.
records.story: In the late 1990s Viña Leyda was founded to plant the dry, wind blown hills of Leyda, west of Santiago and close to the Pacific, where no vines grew. The ground had no water for irrigation, so the founders sought rights to divert water from the Maipo river and laid a pipeline of about eight kilometres to bring it to the hills. The first vineyards went in during 1998, when Leyda was not yet a denomination of origin, and the wines were first labelled within the San Antonio appellation. By its own account the house then led the campaign for a denomination, and in 2002 the Leyda Valley was recognised as a zone of the San Antonio Valley, sharing its name with the house. In 2007 Viña Leyda was sold to the San Pedro wine group. Its Sauvignon Blanc made the zone's name abroad, but Pinot Noir took the hills up as well, and the house built a line of small lots, each drawn from a selection of its plots, at the top of its range. Lot 21 is the Pinot Noir of that line. Here is what the Pacific does to Pinot Noir: it stays light and savoury, with salt where a warmer valley would give jam.

records.place: Rosario valley, between Casablanca and San Antonio, Chile

wine.name: EQ Syrah
wine.sites: The estate's El Rosario vineyard, planted from 1999 in the enclosed Rosario valley under twenty kilometres from the Pacific, on granitic soils, the deeper flats chosen for this wine.
wine.making: After a cold soak of about ten days in small open tanks of two to five tonnes, the grapes ferment with native yeasts, with pumping over and punching down. The malolactic takes place in French oak barrels, where the wine then stays for eighteen to twenty two months, and it rests a year in bottle before release.
wine.glass: Black pepper, blackberry and violet over smoked meat, black olive and a lift of mint; medium bodied and fresh, with fine, firm tannin and a long, peppery finish nearer the northern Rhône than warm valley Syrah.
wine.ageing: Good within a few years of release, it gains bacon fat and dried herbs over ten years and more.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a large Burgundy or Syrah glass.

label.means: The house's estate range, first made with the 2001 harvest.
The house's word for the coastal cool in which its Syrah ripens slowly.

records.table: Granite slopes in the enclosed Rosario valley, under twenty kilometres from the Pacific, carry the biodynamically farmed vines of Matetic's EQ Syrah: black pepper, blackberry and violet with smoked meat, fresher and leaner than warm Chilean Syrah.
records.story: The Matetic family's history in Chile begins in 1892, when a forebear from Fiume, the port that is now Rijeka in Croatia, landed at Punta Arenas in the far south. A century later his descendants turned to wine, and in 1999 they planted their first vineyards in the Rosario valley, a small, enclosed valley of the coastal hills between Casablanca and San Antonio, where cool sea air settles among granite slopes. The first harvest came in 2001 and began the EQ range: Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Syrah. The house describes that first EQ Syrah as Chile's first cool climate Syrah, a claim it makes of itself; it showed at least that Chile's coast could give a Syrah of pepper and freshness in place of the jammy weight of the warm valleys. In 2004, by its own account, the estate gained organic certification and began to farm biodynamically, and all its vineyards later gained Demeter certification. Its EQ Syrah carries the denomination of the San Antonio Valley. Set EQ Syrah beside a Crozes-Hermitage or a Saint-Joseph and Chile's cool coast answers the northern Rhône, while the estate shows what biodynamic farming means on that coast.

records.place: western hills of the Casablanca Valley, Chile

wine.name: Alazán Pinot Noir
wine.sites: Hillside parcels of the family's vineyards in the west of the Casablanca Valley, nearer the sea, on red clay loam over decomposed granite; Alazán is a blend of blocks and lots rather than one parcel.
wine.making: Blocks and lots are made apart and chosen barrel by barrel in the cellar before they are blended. It is aged for about eight to eleven months, by vintage, in French oak barrels, around a third new, with concrete eggs and, in later vintages, Austrian oak foudres: for 2022, half the wine in foudres, two fifths in barrels and a tenth in eggs.
wine.glass: Fresh strawberry, cranberry and rose hip, closing on a savoury, earthy finish that the house likens to baking spice; medium to full in body by its account, silky and taut, with a faint bitterness that lengthens it and alcohol held low.
wine.ageing: By the house's sheets it is released in the September of the year after the harvest, ten months or so out of wood, and is approachable then.
wine.serve: 13 to 15 degrees Celsius; no need to decant a young bottle; a Burgundy glass.

label.means: Spanish for a horse of reddish, copper coat; the house named its flagship for a family horse of that colour.
The coastal valley west of Santiago, planted from 1982 and known first for white wines.

records.table: Blended from barrel selected lots, Alazán is Kingston Family Vineyards' flagship Pinot Noir from red clay and granite hillsides in western Casablanca: strawberry, cranberry and rose hip, low in alcohol, aged in French barrels, concrete eggs and large Austrian casks.
records.story: Early in the twentieth century the family's patriarch left Michigan's Upper Peninsula for Chile to prospect for gold. The mines did not make his fortune, but the family ended with a dairy and cattle ranch in the hills of Casablanca, west of Santiago, and kept it for generations. In 1998, by the family's account, they planted their first vines on the ranch, betting on Pinot Noir and Syrah in a valley then known for white wines. The first harvests were sold to other wineries, but in 2003 the family made its first wine under its own Kingston Family label. The vineyards lie in the western, cooler part of the valley, on hillsides of red clay and decomposed granite, and the house names its wines for the horses of the ranch. Alazán takes its name, by the house's account, from a family horse of deep red coat, and the family chose it for the wine because the wine is deep red too. Alazán and Tobiano were its original Pinot Noir labels, which the house calls its most approachable; its own sheets call Alazán its flagship, and single block wines came later. Alazán is the ranch's answer to whether red Burgundy's grape could ripen in a white wine valley: savoury, low in alcohol and kept fresh by the sea air.

others.name: Tobiano Pinot Noir

traps: Kingston's Pinot Noirs are Casablanca, on the western hills of the valley, not San Antonio or Leyda.
Alazán is the house's flagship Pinot Noir by its own sheets; Tobiano, its other original label, is the lighter one.
Alazán is a blend of barrel selected blocks and lots, not one of the house's single block wines.

cards.front: Kingston Family Vineyards: what was the family's Casablanca land before vines arrived in 1998?
cards.back: A dairy and cattle ranch, kept for generations by a family whose forebear came to Chile prospecting for gold.

cards.front: Kingston's Alazán Pinot Noir: what does its name describe, and why did the family choose it?
cards.back: A horse of reddish coat in Spanish: a family horse of that colour, the wine being deep red too.

questions.q: A guest asks how Kingston Family Vineyards ages its Alazán Pinot Noir in its later vintages. Which answer fits?
opts: French barrels, concrete eggs and Austrian oak foudres
Stainless steel tanks alone, bottled young
New American oak barrels for two full years
Buried clay tinajas for a year and more
questions.exp: The house's sheets give French oak barrels with concrete eggs and, lately, Austrian foudres, for about eight to eleven months; two years in new American oak would bury a cool Pinot Noir.

questions.q: In what year did the Kingston family first plant vines on its Casablanca ranch, by its own account?
questions.exp: The family planted its first vines in 1998; 2003 is the first wine under its own label.

report: Rewritten for Alazán Pinot Noir, the rename the refuter accepted on 2026-11-21; Tobiano now sits in others as the second Pinot Noir.

Alazán as the flagship, the first choice of lots, about a third new French oak and the barrel selection before bottling rest on the house's Pinot Noir page; the vessels on its 2019 and 2022 sheets; eight months in 2016 and 2017 on a trade newsletter's notes, so the record says about eight to ten months.
The name rests on the house's own blog (a family horse of deep red coat; the uncle who owned it is not named, his state unknown); a trade note agrees on a family horse.

The glass joins the house's sheets of 2019, 2021 and 2022 (red fruit, spice, an earthy finish, medium to full body, a subtle bitterness) to the South America Wine Guide's strawberry, cranberry and rose hip. The house's claim of a decade and more in bottle, on its 2020 page alone, is left out of ageing for want of room among the sources.
The first Alazán of 2003 appears only on a writer's own site, so the record gives 2003 as the first own label wine and does not date Alazán's first vintage.
Searches spent on this record: 8 of a share of 14.

changed: wine.making, table, story, others, traps: Alazán from the winemaker's first choice of lots and Tobiano from the next tier stood in no page found in three searches of the house's site, which calls both its original, most approachable Pinot Noir labels made from barrel selected blocks and lots; the tiering is cut and Alazán is now the flagship by the house's 2021 sheet, blended from barrel selected lots.

wine.making and questions[0].exp: was about eight to ten months; now eight to eleven, the 2021 sheet giving eleven, the 2022 sheet ten (half foudre, two fifths barrel, a tenth egg, now stated) and the importer Skurnik eight for 2017.

story: was gold and copper and the family took over a dairy and cattle farm; now gold alone and the family ended with a dairy and cattle ranch, as the sources tell it (copper is only the name of Michigan's Copper Country).
others[0].note: Tobiano's mostly used French oak stood in no source found and is cut.
traps[2]: the single block Cuartel 8D was found in no source and is no longer named.
sources: the horse blog gives way to the house's 2021 sheet, which calls Alazán its flagship; the name's story rests on the house's winemaking page and stays told as the house's account.

integrator, 21 November 2026, wording only: the first card's back still said a dairy and cattle farm taken over by the family, the telling this reading cut from the story; it now says a dairy and cattle ranch kept for generations, as the story has it. The front and its id do not move.
open: The serving line (13 to 15 degrees, a Burgundy glass) is general service for a cool climate Pinot Noir; no sheet of the house gives one.
Grapes sold to other wineries before 2003 rest on the Almanac's report (first harvest 2001) and Wikipedia; the Almanac gives 1997 for the planting, the house 1998.
The house's claim that the wine shows the hillside's micro terroir and the low alcohol (12.5 to 12.6 per cent on the 2019 and 2022 sheets) are its own.
